## Answer

**The privacy gap is real in the pinned stock Hermes configuration with unrestricted tools. It is no longer only an untested possibility.** A local dummy-data probe returned another profile's private transcript through the normal agent tool-invocation path, with the current profile and multiplex secret scope correctly bound. Separate conversation IDs and separate profile directories do not, by themselves, enforce clanker's owner/audience contract.

This does **not** establish that ordinary conversations spontaneously leak, that a live reviewer has accessed another reviewer's data, or that every possible shared-process configuration is unsafe. Slack routing and normal profile-state separation have useful working controls. A shared Slack bot can remain. A permanent full runtime per user has not been shown to be the only solution.

## Scope and evidence standard

- Audited the installed, clean upstream checkout at `f97608f178d1ffeca59860195ab7da295f7c8e5f`, release `v2026.9.24`, Hermes `0.21.5`. All source references below refer to that commit, not an assumed current `main`.
- Read the pinned documentation/source and checked the live official [profile](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/profiles/) and [multiplexing](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/developer-guide/multiplexing-gateway/) documentation. The latter explicitly separates profile scoping from end-user authorization.
- Traced Slack identity, route selection, turn scope, agent tool dispatch, memory, recall, terminal/files/code, browser/vault state, result delivery and owner approval. Independent reviews are linked below.
- Ran synthetic behavior probes with temporary dummy state. No real Slack connection, real private account, live browser login, model inference or external publication was used.
- A source finding identifies behavior in a call path. A local reproduction proves only the exercised component/path. Neither is a hosted end-to-end acceptance result.

## Findings at a glance

| Boundary | Finding | Evidence strength | Smallest response to evaluate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slack DM versus shared thread | Correct tenant/session keys and runtime-profile scope exist. Broad sender routes also select the sender's private profile in shared channels; unmatched routes use the receiving bot's default profile. | Source, upstream tests, dummy route probes | Exact workspace + DM-channel routes, separate authorized shared context, strict admission, unprivileged fallback. |
| Memory within one profile | Built-in memory is loaded into new conversations from the profile's files; separate DM/channel sessions do not create a separate memory owner. | Source and actual memory/prompt-assembly probe | Separate private and audience contexts, or a verified audience-aware memory implementation. |
| Recall across profiles | The model may name another installed profile, including inside a session reference. The tool opens its database without checking the current user's ownership. | Source, real invocation-path probe, upstream test explicitly expecting the behavior | Disable unrestricted recall or supply enforced current-context recall. Cover both profile arguments and embedded profile references. |
| Browser and saved account access | Vault authority is profile-scoped. Several browser persistence/naming modes intentionally share state within a profile; the real-profile CDP cache also has a process-global slot. | Source and bounded dummy vault/cache probes | Separate owner/audience profiles; choose and verify browser/backend persistence deliberately; constrain selectable sessions and avoid shared real-profile attachment. |
| Arbitrary execution and publication | Local execution has the server account's permissions. Docker can contain terminal/files/code but does not automatically constrain every host-side tool or copied transcript. Native outbound messaging and shared approval cards do not supply owner-approved publication semantics. | Source; local execution/approval probes in supporting reports | Actual execution isolation plus constrained host tools, protected shared stores, and an owner/content/audience-bound publishing path. |

## 1. Slack routing is useful and configurable

Authenticated Slack events supply workspace and sender identity. The runner distinguishes the bot receiving the event from the profile executing it and freezes that decision. Workspace IDs enter Slack session keys. Two users can contribute to one shared thread while their DMs remain separate.

Relevant paths:

- `plugins/platforms/slack/adapter.py:1749-1822,3481-3497,4471-4588`: bot authentication, event workspace/sender and source construction.
- `gateway/session_identity.py:240-272`: transport/runtime identity resolution.
- `gateway/run_adapters.py:1559-1566`: entry into the routed profile's runtime scope.
- `gateway/session.py:644-714`: profile/tenant/chat/thread session keys.
- `gateway/profile_routing.py:58-101`: conjunctive route matching and specificity.
- `gateway/run.py:4437-4487`: route selection, served-profile check, unmatched fallback.

The route trap is concrete: a rule for `workspace + Sahan -> sahan-private` outranks a rule for `workspace + shared-channel -> team`. Sahan's shared-channel request consequently runs with his private profile. A channel reply can then be generated using private context. The routing probe reproduced profile selection; it did not generate a real leaked reply.

For the fixed demo workspace, explicit DM-channel routes can avoid this. A shared profile must correspond to the actual permitted audience: unrelated private channels must not share one global memory/recall store merely because they belong to the same workspace.

Strict bot admission is separate from route matching. An unmatched admitted event falls back; route tables alone do not reject every unknown tenant/sender/audience tuple. An explicit reliable admission check may still be needed. Group DMs also require deliberate handling: the pinned Slack adapter emits `chat_type='dm'` for MPIMs, which some downstream helpers treat as private. See the [Slack audit](audit-slack-notes.md).

## 2. One profile for all users fails the memory boundary

`tools/memory_tool.py:38-40` resolves memory to the active profile's `memories/` directory. `agent/agent_init.py:1259-1296` loads the built-in store, enabled by default. `agent/system_prompt.py:515-524` inserts that store into the system prompt without choosing separate files for the Slack sender or channel audience.

The probe wrote an ordinary dummy private fact into one profile's memory, loaded a fresh store, and called the actual prompt-memory assembly helper for a shared-conversation agent. The fact appeared in the generated prompt block. This does not depend on persuading a model to perform an unauthorized file read. It establishes exposure to the model once a private fact has entered shared-profile memory; it does not claim every DM fact is automatically memorized.

A positive-control probe bound a distinct team profile and confirmed its normal memory loading did not include Alice's marker. **Separate profiles help normal state selection.** The next finding shows why that alone is insufficient against deliberate tool access.

## 3. Cross-profile recall is reproduced through the agent invocation path

The relevant call chain is:

```text
agent_runtime_helpers.invoke_tool
  -> request middleware / pre_tool_call hooks
  -> INLINE_TOOL_EXECUTORS["session_search"]
  -> session_search(... profile=model_argument, db=current_profile_db ...)
  -> _dispatch (also extracts profile from profile/session reference)
  -> _resolve_profile_db
  -> open named profile's state.db read-only
  -> return that transcript
```

Pinned source:

- `agent/agent_runtime_helpers.py:2367-2446`: invocation/middleware/hooks.
- `agent/inline_tool_executors.py:121-137`: forwards the model's `profile` and `session_id` along with the current database.
- `tools/session_search_tool.py:434-444`: validates the profile name and existence, then opens its database; no requester/owner comparison.
- `tools/session_search_tool.py:577-605`: adopts an embedded profile, swaps to the selected database, and reads/browses it.
- `toolsets.py:25-26`: memory and recall are in the core tool bundle, subject to normal tool selection.

The outer normal tool path does not supply a missing owner check: `agent/tool_executor.py:403-457` checks tool-bridge selection/schema; `651-720` applies plugins and loop guardrails. Those guards do not equate a selected profile with an authorized owner.

The local probe used actual temporary SQLite session stores. Bob's home override was active, multiplex secret handling was enabled, and a scoped empty secret mapping was installed. Calling the normal `invoke_tool` entry point returned Alice's dummy transcript with either:

```json
{"profile":"alice","session_id":"alice-private"}
{"session_id":"alice/alice-private"}
```

No LLM was involved. The agent object's database handle/identity was represented by a small fixture, while the invocation, middleware/hook dispatch, inline executor, database resolution and reads used upstream implementations. This demonstrates the available capability when unrestricted recall is enabled, not a complete Slack attack.

The positive control passed: a bare unknown session ID without another profile did **not** scan other profiles. Ordinary default selection and explicit cross-profile access are different behaviors.

Upstream has a [test specifically requiring named-profile recall](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/f97608f178d1ffeca59860195ab7da295f7c8e5f/tests/agent/test_inline_session_search_profile.py). It passed locally. This is useful personal-agent functionality that conflicts with clanker's untrusted-user boundary when exposed unrestricted.

Reproduction: [probe source](probes/test_profile_boundary.py), [captured result](evidence/2026-10-03-profile-boundary-probes.txt). Six local behavior probes and the upstream test passed. Four local probe cases witness exposure capabilities; two confirm narrower existing separation. **These green probes are not green privacy acceptance tests.**

## 4. Account/browser authority follows profiles and backend semantics

The pinned release contains the credential vault; these findings do not rely on vault code from a newer commit. Vault entries and external-vault unlock tokens are scoped to the Hermes home, not separately to each Slack sender. A browser task ID does not add an owner field to a vault entry. Origin checks prevent filling credentials on the wrong website; they do not decide which human may use a saved login for the correct website.

The browser/vault review reproduced a second session in the same profile listing a dummy login, reusing a dummy external-vault unlock token, and reaching the fill boundary with that login. Browser socket interaction was replaced with a fake. Separate profile homes gave separate normal vault/token visibility.

Browser identity is backend-specific. Named Browser Use sessions can override per-task separation within a profile; persistent Camofox identity is shared within a profile by design. Real-profile attachment uses a process-global CDP cache; a dummy cache probe demonstrated reuse across home scopes. This last observation is a cache-level reproduction, not evidence of an actual cross-user browser session having been driven.

There is also an execution distinction: `browser_exec` runs Python through a **host subprocess**, even if that Python controls a remote browser. `model_tools.py:391-395` explicitly documents host execution and hides this tool when terminal capability is absent; `tools/browser_use_cli.py:594-600,612-662` launches it directly. Selecting Docker for the terminal does not reroute this separate launch into that Docker environment. Keeping this path enabled requires isolating its host execution or changing the execution path; an alternative is a constrained browser tool/backend that preserves the required browser workflow. This is source evidence, not a live Browser Use execution test.

Detailed source references, controls and bounded reproduction evidence are in the [browser/vault audit](audit-browser-notes.md).

## 5. Execution isolation and sharing need explicit enforcement

Profiles are not OS sandboxes. The default local terminal executes with the host account's permissions, as both the [official documentation](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/profiles/#profiles-vs-workspaces-vs-sandboxing) and source describe.

An important qualification: the pinned file tools and `execute_code` do follow the selected remote terminal backend. It would be incorrect to say they always run on the host even after Docker is selected. Docker can therefore close a substantial part of the file/code boundary if its mounts, users and lifecycle are appropriate. Persistent Docker defaults to one container per profile, shared by that profile's sessions, so the profile mapping still matters.

Other handlers, including recall and memory, execute in the Hermes host process. A terminal container alone does not constrain the cross-profile database read reproduced above. A full runtime container with all users' data mounted together would also retain the problem. Every accessible store and tool must follow the chosen trust boundary.

Private final replies are copied into the launch home's delivery ledger for recovery (`gateway/delivery_ledger.py:171-184,270-283`). That is not itself an end-user leak. It means a worker must not have unrestricted access to this shared store, even if each profile's primary session database is separate.

For publication, native Slack `send_message` accepts a model-selected destination without an owner/content/audience approval record. Shared Slack approval buttons check whether the clicker may use the bot, not whether they own the private action. A dummy handler probe allowed another admitted user to reach the resolver. Private DM controls restrict visibility, but stock shared cards do not establish the required ownership check.

Detailed paths and probe limits: [execution audit](audit-execution-notes.md), [Slack audit](audit-slack-notes.md).

## What this establishes for the design

1. **Reject a single shared profile for reviewers' private accounts and shared context.** Independent chat sessions are not enough for profile-scoped memory, vault and browser persistence.
2. **Use explicit private and audience profile routing.** Keep unknown routes unprivileged and verify tenant admission. This reuses existing Hermes machinery.
3. **Constrain every cross-context access path.** Disable unrestricted recall or replace it with enforced scoped recall; choose an isolated browser backend; constrain arbitrary execution and host-side tools. Disabling a feature is acceptable only if the required product experience still works.
4. **Provide owner-bound private work and publication.** If a shared task needs private account work, keep its observations private and release only approved content to an approved audience. Stock general-purpose outbound tools/shared approval cards do not prove this flow.
5. **Select the smallest enforceable deployment after checking the active tool inventory.** A shared trusted gateway plus correctly isolated tools may suffice. Separate whole runtimes are an alternative if host-side access cannot be constrained reliably. The evidence does not mandate a permanent instance per person.

Plugin hooks are a possible implementation seam, not automatic proof of enforcement. The actual pre-tool callback dispatcher blocks callback errors/timeouts; some outer error handling and the gateway-dispatch hook are fail-open. A policy must have reliable identity, complete path coverage and defined failure behavior. Inspecting shell strings is not a substitute for execution isolation.

**Configuration-only remains a candidate for a restricted tool set.** Separate audience profiles, private Docker mounts, unrestricted recall disabled, no host Python browser path or shared authenticated CDP endpoint, inline skill shell off, and constrained outbound tools can remove the demonstrated paths. This audit does not prove that every such stock configuration fails. It also does not verify one that preserves every v1 feature. Automated private-to-shared publication still needs enforceable owner/content/audience mediation; a manual workflow must not silently replace required behavior.

## Recorded checks

| Check | Result | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Seven selected routing/identity/approval/delivery test files | 40 upstream tests passed | Synthetic upstream fixtures; see [captured output](evidence/2026-10-03-slack-audit-tests.txt). |
| Upstream named-profile recall test | 1 passed | Confirms upstream intentionally supports cross-profile recall. |
| Local memory/recall probes | 6 passed as behavior witnesses | Four exposure cases and two positive controls; not privacy acceptance. |
| Slack route/approval/MPIM probe | Expected findings reproduced | Fake transport/resolver; [source](probes/slack_boundary_probe.py), [observations](evidence/2026-10-03-slack-boundary-probe.json). |
| Vault/browser probe | 12 observations matched | Dummy vaults/tokens and mocked browser/cache boundaries; [source](probes/browser_vault_ownership.py), [observations](evidence/browser_vault_ownership.json). |
| Filesystem/dispatch/policy probe | Read and policy behaviors reproduced | Dummy files, real dispatch and callback handling; see [execution report](audit-execution-notes.md). |

The upstream tracked checkout remained unchanged. Only research notes, probe sources and sanitized evidence were added to clanker's repository.

## Remaining uncertainty

Live Slack/model/browser behavior, concurrent authenticated tasks, browser backend deployment, real access lifecycle and hosted restart recovery remain unverified. No source audit can establish that a model will never select a dangerous tool argument. Here, the acceptance concern is already decidable: the required forbidden access is currently available through an enabled stock capability. Fixing or removing that capability does not require waiting for an accidental leak.

The next engineering decision is which active tools and shared/private deployment boundary to retain. This report does not change `production/V1_SCOPE.md`, adopt a new architecture, or implement any fixes.
"}}

# clanker v1 scope and build approach Historical production scope. [POC_SCOPE.md](../POC_SCOPE.md) records the local setup and remaining reviewer checks; the hosted design below remains the broader v1 roadmap. ## State **clanker v1 is a hosted Hermes-based Slack assistant for general browser tasks and access management. Reuse Hermes first; focus clanker-specific work on routing and authorization, and add code only for demonstrated gaps.** The repository contains this scope, a verification strategy and source review, plus a pinned stock Hermes local baseline and clanker Slack setup files. The local CLI starts, 47 targeted upstream routing/session tests pass, and real Slack owner commands work in a DM and the test channel; see [LOCAL_BASELINE.md](../verification/LOCAL_BASELINE.md). The full Slack/browser E2E, deployed reviewer experience, and v1 acceptance remain open. Upstream documentation and synthetic tests establish narrower capabilities, not that our chosen deployment has passed its requirements. **Selected browser architecture:** each assigned worker VM runs Hermes and local Chromium, controlled through Hermes's existing Browser Use driver. This is the selected v1 design; the VM pool, browser workflow, and persistence across VM replacement still require implementation and verification. **Selected access interface:** a hosted clanker vault web app uses Sign in with Slack to collect and manage saved access. Reuse Hermes's vault implementation and UI/API components behind clanker's authenticated owner and task checks. This integration is selected, not implemented or verified. The assignment permits third-party components and prioritizes a smooth working experience over code volume. A successful v1 may consist mostly of configuration, deployment, integration fixes, and verification. There is no requirement to build a new agent harness, Slack connector, browser engine, vault, or TOTP algorithm. Slack is the v1 conversation interface, with the hosted vault web app for secure access collection and management. The user reported that Sahan approved Slack identity replacing the assignment's Google-only chatbot sign-in requirement. Sahan and Nishank enter through the demo workspace invitation/entry link and use clanker without local setup or their own model-provider accounts. Inference is owner-funded. The assignment's core is browser tasks and secure access management. Private DMs, shared channel context, and protection between reviewers are additional v1 behavior requested by the user. A general self-service SaaS platform is not a prerequisite. ### Preferred inference setup: owner's ChatGPT account Prefer using the owner's existing ChatGPT subscription through Hermes's ChatGPT/Codex OAuth provider for the cloud baseline, to avoid purchasing separate API credits for eligible model usage. Reviewers still use Slack without their own model-provider accounts. This is the preferred setup to evaluate, not a verified funding arrangement. [Hermes documents](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/integrations/providers) device-code authorization, which lets the owner approve login in their browser while Hermes runs and stores its authentication on the cloud host. [OpenAI documents](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001542-using-your-chatgpt-plan-in-other-apps-and-sites) eligible plan usage in supported integrations; Hermes's exact account eligibility and quota accounting remain unverified for this deployment. Before relying on this route, establish that the intended owner-funded reviewer usage is supported, run a small inference request, and inspect the resulting usage and billing. Verify authentication refresh and persistence across a cloud restart with the owner's laptop out of the execution path. Subscription-funded inference does not establish coverage for hosting or separately billed browser/tool services. Record those costs separately. Any alternative paid inference setup remains a separate decision if the preferred route cannot meet the requirements. ## Reuse from Hermes Pin the Hermes version and required integrations, configure them, and verify their behavior in the deployed Slack experience. | Capability | Starting point | What clanker must establish | | --- | --- | --- | | Agent harness | Hermes's agent loop, tools, skills, and session machinery | General tasks work with the selected model and enabled tools. | | Slack interface | Hermes's existing Slack adapter and gateway | App configuration, authenticated admission, correct conversation routing, and replies. | | Browser automation | Local Chromium inside the assigned worker VM, controlled by Hermes's existing Browser Use driver (`browser_exec`) | Background browser work, uploads/downloads, secure login/handoff, scoped browser persistence, and saved-access reuse across worker replacement. | | Credentials and 2FA | Hermes's credential vault, Desktop vault form/API components, protected browser filling, TOTP support, and access-management controls | The hosted clanker vault web app authenticates with Slack and enforces owner/task/site access before saving or using credentials. Reviewers can securely provide, reuse, and remove access. Resolve the TOTP choice below. | | Profiles and conversations | Existing profile routing, DM/channel/thread sessions, memory, and persistence | The selected configuration enforces the intended tenant, owner, and audience boundaries across turns and restarts. | Start from the documented [browser integration](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/browser/), [credential vault](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/credential-vault/), [profile routing](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/multi-profile-gateways/#routing-shared-bot-chats-to-profiles-profile_routes), and [session behavior](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/sessions/#shared-vs-isolated-group-sessions). Native vault UI/API components cover CLI/Desktop use; the selected hosted web app adds the Slack identity and access-request authorization boundary. The complete collection, reuse, and revocation flow still needs validation. ## Architecture and routing contract **Use a shared Slack gateway and a pool of isolated Hermes worker VMs.** The gateway binds authenticated tenant, sender, and conversation audience to an authorized profile before queueing the task. The scheduler assigns a ready VM to that private or shared context; the VM pool manager maintains clean warm spares, adds capacity within limits, and removes excess idle capacity. Each worker runs Hermes, its Browser Use driver, and local Chromium inside the same VM. Profiles and permitted browser/file state persist beyond the worker's lifetime. The hosting provider, pool sizes, idle timeout, and storage implementation remain open choices. ```mermaid flowchart TD Slack["Slack workspaces
Private DMs and shared channels/threads"] <--> Gateway["Hermes Slack gateway"] Gateway --> Routing["Authenticated tenant, sender, and audience
Bind authorized profile and task"] Routing --> Queue["Durable task queue + scheduler
Fair dispatch, leases, bounded retries"] Queue -->|Assign task| Worker["Assigned worker VM
Hermes + Browser Use driver + local Chromium
One authorized private or shared context"] Queue -->|Pending demand| Pool["VM pool manager / autoscaler
Ready-spare target, VM limits, idle timeout"] Pool -->|Lifecycle calls| Provider["VM provider API"] Provider -->|Provision or stop| Worker Worker -->|Capacity and health| Pool Worker <--> Access["Enforced resource access
Only the current context's authorized state"] Access <--> State["Durable profile home, browser state, and files
Separate task and delivery records"] Gateway -->|Private access link| VaultUI["Hosted clanker vault web app"] VaultUI <--> Auth["Sign in with Slack
OIDC identity + server session"] Auth -->|Verified workspace and user| Trusted["Trusted credential handler
Owner, task, site, and action checks"] VaultUI -->|Secure credential submission| Trusted Trusted <--> Vault["Protected durable Hermes vault
Keys inaccessible to agent code"] Access -->|Authorized credential operation| Trusted Trusted -->|Resume after durable save| Queue Worker -->|Persist result| Delivery["Result delivery + owner-bound approval enforcement"] Delivery --> Gateway ``` These boxes describe responsibilities, not mandatory separate services. Reuse Hermes's Slack adapter, agent runtime, browser driver, vault, and session machinery. Routing checks may use existing configuration, supported extension points, or a small clanker integration. The scheduler and VM pool manager can share a backend service. The remote worker-to-gateway handoff must bind and durably record results before releasing a worker; reuse existing Slack delivery where it fits. Run Hermes in its upstream runtime; TypeScript remains the preference for clanker-owned integration code where appropriate. ### Selected browser stack: local Chromium + Browser Use Use the existing [Browser Use driver](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/browser/#browser-use-mode-default) with local Chromium. Hermes remains the agent making decisions; Browser Use supplies browser control through `browser_exec`. A hosted browser service is not part of the selected v1 baseline. Make local selection explicit instead of relying on credential autodetection: ```yaml browser: cloud_provider: local backend: browser-use ``` Build the worker image with pinned, compatible versions of Hermes, the Browser Use CLI, `agent-browser`, Chromium, and the required Linux dependencies. The pinned Hermes release installs/discovers the Browser Use CLI separately; pinning Hermes alone does not pin that driver. Complete installation during image construction so assigned tasks do not depend on first-use downloads. Keep **Hermes itself, the Python executed by `browser_exec`, and Chromium inside the assigned VM**. Running only the browser there would leave driver code executing on the shared host. Expose only the current context's authorized profile, browser state, and files; a shared channel worker must not receive a participant's private account state. Persist the authorized profile state, including `state.db` conversation and tool history, plus the dedicated browser profile and required workspace files/artifacts. Keep the protected vault and its decryption keys outside agent-accessible profile mounts, as specified below. Clanker's task record references the Hermes profile and session rather than duplicating chat history. Default local Chromium sessions are temporary, so configure and verify a persistent browser profile; a dedicated local Chromium instance connected through CDP is an existing integration option. The exact persistence mechanism remains to be validated. Restoring conversation history and cookies does not by itself restore a live page, unfinished form, or in-flight action. Before accepting this stack, exercise secure credential filling and human login/handoff, saved-login reuse in a fresh browser, saved-session reuse separately, download/inspection or transformation/upload, owner/audience separation, revocation, and recovery after worker replacement. These are pending acceptance checks, not capabilities already verified in clanker's local baseline. ### Selected access flow: hosted vault + Sign in with Slack Send the owner a private link to an expiring access request. The hosted clanker vault web app authenticates with Slack OpenID Connect and can reuse a valid server session for later visits. Validate the token signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and nonce, and validate OAuth state on the redirect. Match the verified Slack `team_id` and `user_id` to the request's tenant and owner; the server also binds the task, site origin, and permitted action. Reject a mismatched identity, expired request, or replay, and consume the request once on successful submission. Neither an email address, URL parameter, nor possession of the link grants access. This Sign in with Slack flow is separate from the Slack bot installation OAuth flow. Reuse Hermes's vault storage, validation, browser-fill/TOTP primitives, and existing Desktop form/API components where suitable. Clanker supplies the hosted page, authenticated session, request authorization, and task-resumption integration; exposing the general Hermes dashboard or accepting a client-selected profile is not that boundary. The existing optional setup-key field is reusable capability, not a decision to enable automatic TOTP; the product choice below remains unresolved. Submit secrets directly from the secure form to a trusted credential handler. Passwords and setup keys must bypass Slack, model inputs, task queue payloads, and application logs. The handler selects authorized storage from trusted identity, persists it durably, and returns only a handle and safe metadata. Keep the handler and decryption keys in an execution boundary inaccessible to arbitrary agent code; a context-local profile switch or a vault key beside agent-readable files does not enforce this. Authorized browser filling uses the protected path without returning the secret to the model. The exact boundary and Hermes integration require implementation and verification. Persist `waiting_for_input` and the access request independently of the worker VM. After a successful durable save, atomically consume the request and record the task's readiness for resumption, with idempotent dispatch so retries cannot lose or duplicate the resume transition. Requeue the original task with the credential handle, not the secret; an active worker need not remain online while the owner fills the form. Verify that saving during worker replacement resumes the correct task and that removing access prevents further affected credential use and saved-session reuse. | Routing decision | Required behavior | | --- | --- | | Tenant | Derive workspace/installation identity from authenticated Slack events. Include it in user, conversation, and resource routing. Reject unknown or unauthorized requesters instead of falling into a privileged default. | | Conversation and audience | A 1:1 DM loads that user's private context. A channel/thread loads context authorized for that channel's audience. Workspace membership alone does not reveal private-channel history. | | Requester and resource owner | Keep the sender, account/resource owner, and conversation audience distinct. Validate ownership before using credentials, browsers, files, history, or controls. Another participant's follow-up conveys no authority over someone else's private work. | | Context and tools | Scope memory, session recall, learned skills, files, artifacts, browser state, and credentials to the current authorized context. Prompt instructions and model-supplied owner IDs cannot grant access. | | Result destination | Return private account results privately. Sharing requires the owner's approval of the specific content and audience. Shared output grants no access to its source account or private files. | Session separation and profile routing are useful controls, but must be tested together with tools and persistence. Shared-profile memory or session recall must not expose DM content in a channel. Model-generated code must not have unrestricted access to other owners' files, the shared history store, or platform administrator credentials. Use supported scoped tools and isolated execution where needed; disable or adapt a tool whose access cannot be constrained. Keep retained history, recovery state, browser access, and artifacts durable across restarts, with their owner/audience associations intact. Use existing persistence when it meets these needs. The VM execution boundary and local browser stack above are selected; the cloud vendor, storage technology, and exact profile/session mapping remain implementation choices. For v1 delivery, the reviewers use one demo workspace. Routing must still carry tenant identity and be checked against another tenant identity without requiring a public onboarding or provisioning product. ### Example: collaboration involving a private account Sahan and Nishank discuss a report in a shared thread. Both contributions belong to that thread's context. If the work needs Sahan's private account, route that part into an owner-authorized private conversation/run, using existing capabilities where possible. Obtain missing authorization through his DM or secure handoff. Private observations never enter the shared conversation automatically. Sahan receives the result privately and may approve selected content for publication back into the thread. Nishank can continue the shared discussion without gaining authority over Sahan's account. ## Required behavior 1. **Perform general browser and file tasks.** Accept natural-language goals across different, unfamiliar websites. Discover and upload an intended existing file; support download, inspection/transformation, and upload when requested. Site-specific scripts are not evidence of general capability. 2. **Collect, reuse, and revoke access.** Support secure input or login handoff for passwords, API keys, OAuth/browser access, and card details when needed. Keep secrets out of chat and model inputs. Reuse encrypted saved access and browser sessions across tasks and fresh browser runs. Owners can remove access; affected active work and saved sessions must not silently retain the revoked authority. 3. **Preserve private and shared boundaries.** DMs, personal memory, credentials, browser state, and private files stay owner-scoped. Channel discussions and intentionally shared material stay audience-scoped. Concurrent users cannot take over each other's sessions, account access, private history, approvals, or artifacts. 4. **Work in the background and recover.** Acknowledge requests promptly, provide useful brief progress, clarify material details, and offer private human handoff when needed. Persist the task through expired access, failures, and restarts; resume without blindly replaying completed consequential actions. Support cancellation and bounded execution. 5. **Confirm and verify.** Obtain owner confirmation for concrete consequential actions such as purchases, external messages, publication, or deletion. Changed action details require fresh confirmation. Confirm the actual website state or artifact before reporting completion. Approval for an action and approval to share its private result are separate permissions. ### TOTP: existing capability, unresolved product choice Reuse Hermes's existing TOTP implementation if automatic generation is included. The user's preferred flow is to supply the current code through secure input or a private browser handoff, keeping the setup key with the user. The original assignment explicitly requires accepting a TOTP setup key once and generating subsequent codes. **Manual code entry alone does not satisfy that criterion.** Resolve whether to demonstrate native automatic TOTP with the user's agreement or obtain an accepted assignment exception before declaring v1 complete. Automatic generation as an opt-in was discussed as a possibility, not settled. This choice does not require implementing a new TOTP algorithm and does not block the initial Slack/browser/routing proof. ## Now: build in this order 1. **Configure the selected local browser worker.** Pin Hermes and its browser dependencies, prepare a worker VM image with local Chromium and the Browser Use driver, enable the existing browser/vault capabilities, and provide reproducible setup and secret-free environment examples. Verify the chosen profile, browser, and workspace persistence arrangement. 2. **Configure routing and the secure access handoff.** Map verified workspace and sender identities to private DM or shared channel context and the correct resources. Build the selected vault web app and Slack sign-in flow around existing Hermes components, with owner-bound access requests and durable task resumption. Verify a two-user example, including denial of another user's access link. 3. **Exercise the complete reviewer flow.** From Slack, request browser work, provide access securely, reuse it, complete the file workflow, handle a failure, and remove access. Check shared collaboration and private boundaries using the actual enabled tools. Record passes, failures, and untested behavior. 4. **Fix remaining demonstrated gaps.** Prefer configuration, then supported plugins/extensions, then small integration changes beyond the selected hosted access flow. Validate owner-bound resource selection and controlled result delivery instead of rebuilding passing upstream features. 5. **Validate the hosted experience and package the result.** Repeat the acceptance checks with the developer's laptop out of the execution path. Produce the repository, entry link, demo, and access-management note. Attribute Hermes and other reused components accurately. **Done when:** the required behavior works through the deployed reviewer experience, the four deliverables exist, and the release evidence passes. Code volume and the number of custom components are not completion criteria. Record unsupported or unresolved requirements explicitly; do not mark v1 complete while they remain unmet. ## Release evidence | Area | Evidence required | | --- | --- | | Inference authentication and funding | Verify the chosen ChatGPT/Codex OAuth route supports the owner's account and intended hosted reviewer use. Record observed model-usage accounting and any separate charges. Exercise authentication refresh and restart persistence without depending on the owner's laptop. If this route is unavailable, record the unmet setup choice and agree an alternative before relying on it. | | General browser and file work | Complete real tasks on at least two different websites using the selected local Chromium + Browser Use stack inside the worker VM. Record driver/browser versions and confirm execution uses the local browser. Verify destination state independently of the agent's completion message. Find and upload the intended existing file, and complete download/inspection or transformation/upload. Treat two websites as an initial proof, not universal coverage. | | Access lifecycle | A reviewer signs into the hosted vault with Slack, securely connects access, and removes it. Reject wrong-user/wrong-workspace, expired, replayed, or altered access requests. Show secrets bypass chat/model/queue/logs and arbitrary agent code cannot read the vault's decryption keys. Verify durable save and resumption across worker replacement, saved-credential reuse in a fresh browser, saved-session reuse separately, and revocation of further affected access. Resolve and verify the TOTP criterion above. | | Recovery and durability | Exercise expired access or a controlled failure, supply the required input, and resume the original task. Restart the runtime and retain the correct history and artifacts. Verify recovery does not duplicate a completed consequential action. | | Routing, privacy, and collaboration | Two reviewers contribute to a shared task and retain its authorized context after restart. Test simultaneous private work, forged owner/tenant references, cross-user files/history/memory/skills, another participant's follow-up, and copied controls. Check that routing, enabled tools, and persisted data uphold the boundary, including another tenant identity. Demonstrate an approved result shared to a channel while private source data remains protected. | | Approvals and honest completion | Another participant cannot approve the owner's private action; changed action details or sharing audiences cannot reuse an old approval. Record actual outcomes, human intervention, failures, relevant versions, and known limits. Distinguish configured, verified, unsupported, and untested capabilities. | ## Four deliverables | Deliverable | Completion criteria | | --- | --- | | Runnable repository | Pinned dependencies/upstream versions, configuration, setup instructions, secret-free environment examples, and exercised verification instructions. Include integration code only where needed. | | Deployed reviewer experience | Slack invitation/entry link and hosted execution available without the developer's laptop. Two reviewers can use it without local setup or their own model-provider account. | | Approximately two-minute yyoreel demo | A real request, secure access collection or handoff, and verified completion. Include reuse/recovery where practical; inspect the exported video for exposed secrets before sharing. | | Access-management and known-limits note | Explain the chosen routing/profile/session boundaries, storage, access collection/reuse/revocation, TOTP decision, recovery, and verified limits. Identify upstream functionality versus clanker changes and explicitly disclose deferred operator/provider privacy controls. | ## Later Self-service multi-tenant onboarding/provisioning, additional messaging interfaces, delegated account access, advanced cross-team memory/grants, and configurable approval-policy UX are outside v1. Basic shared channel context, private DMs, ordinary owner confirmations, and approved result sharing remain in v1. Operator-access and model-provider-access privacy controls, including broader auditing, retention, training-use, and data-lifecycle controls, are deferred to clanker v2 or later as requested. This does not defer credential secrecy, protection between users/tenants, or honest disclosure of the deployed system's limits. ## Next Configure the selected local Chromium + Browser Use worker with Hermes's existing access capabilities, then prove the two-user DM/channel routing behavior and first complete browser task through Slack. Verify persistence across worker replacement and use those results to determine the remaining integration work. Settle the remaining TOTP choice before final acceptance. Obtain the user's review before external submission or contacting the founders. # Clanker operator setup This guide accompanies the [README](../README.md). It describes the current local POC. Runtime installation is documented; complete browser activation on a clean machine still needs verification. The older [Slack setup](../verification/SLACK_SETUP.md) records the original owner-only baseline and should not replace the current membership configuration below. ## Runtime and model Install the pinned environment using the README's commands. The launcher creates `.local/hermes-lab/home/config.yaml` from the initial baseline only if it does not already exist. It also creates a mode-600 `.env`. Configure inference interactively with `scripts/hermes-lab model`, preserving `auth.adopt_external_logins: false`. Current development uses `gpt-6.1-sol` through `openai-codex`. A new operator must authorize their own eligible account or choose another Hermes-supported provider. Do not copy development authentication into a submission or another installation. ## Slack app and membership Create the app from the [manifest](../verification/slack-app-manifest.json), enable Socket Mode, create an app-level token with `connections:write`, and install the bot in the intended workspace. Put the real tokens only in the local `.env`: ```dotenv SLACK_BOT_TOKEN=REPLACE_LOCALLY_WITH_BOT_TOKEN SLACK_APP_TOKEN=REPLACE_LOCALLY_WITH_SOCKET_MODE_TOKEN ``` Merge this configuration into `.local/hermes-lab/home/config.yaml`, replacing both ID placeholders. Preserve the model and baseline security/display settings: ```yaml gateway: multiplex_profiles: true platforms: slack: skip_context_files: true slack: require_mention: true unauthorized_dm_behavior: ignore platforms: slack: enabled: true gateway_restart_notification: false typing_indicator: true extra: allow_admin_from: - OPERATOR_MEMBER_ID group_allow_admin_from: - OPERATOR_MEMBER_ID user_allowed_commands: - status - stop group_user_allowed_commands: - status - stop reactions: true acknowledgement_reactions: true workspace_membership: enabled: true workspace_id: WORKSPACE_TEAM_ID platform_toolsets: cli: [] slack: [] ``` Starting with empty toolsets keeps chat available while execution is being prepared. The verified execution plugin supplies `clanker_browser` only after activation; adding that name by itself does not install or verify a browser. For a fresh installation, the controller provisions eligible current workspace members into new profiles. The configured workspace and current channel/bot membership govern admission; an old owner-only `SLACK_ALLOWED_USERS` or channel allowlist can prevent the intended member experience. Review existing restrictions deliberately rather than blindly replacing a production configuration. The manifest subscribes to `team_join`, `user_change`, `member_joined_channel` and `member_left_channel`, which the membership controller handles. Slack documents the [member-join](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/events/team_join/), [member-change](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/events/user_change/), [channel-join](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/events/member_joined_channel/) and [channel-leave](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/events/member_left_channel/) events. Their required scopes are already in the manifest. A local manifest edit does not update an installed Slack app. Invite the app to the intended demo channels. Workspace identity is the admission boundary: this configuration enables eligible members of that workspace, not just the operator. Use a dedicated demo workspace. ## Local browser execution The tested dependency versions are listed in the README. Browser Use, agent-browser, Node and Chromium must already be installed. These scripts wire executables and policies; they do not download the browser stack: ```sh .local/hermes-lab/venv/bin/python scripts/prepare-clanker-browser --help .local/hermes-lab/venv/bin/python scripts/prepare-clanker-execution --help ``` `prepare-clanker-browser` needs the protected gateway home and absolute paths to the four installed executables. It prepares existing member/channel profiles and prints the path to a receipt. `prepare-clanker-execution` consumes that receipt and installs Seatbelt-backed contexts without granting Slack tools. Activation also requires current-policy acceptance. The existing `verification/probes/seatbelt_boundary_probe.py` and `scripts/enable-clanker-browser` depend on development profile names, paths and receipts, and the older boundary probe expects an earlier tool inventory. They are not a portable clean-install command. Adapt the acceptance harness for a new host, verify file/control-access denials and browser readiness, then activate the verified fleet. This reproducibility gap remains on the submission checklist. The launcher restores the public-web egress broker when the fleet exists. Missing or unaccepted execution policy must leave browser tools unavailable. The [execution decision](decisions/2026-10-05-local-execution-boundary.md) records the tested boundary and its limits. ## Hosted vault After the gateway has created `slack_membership.json`, expose its loopback vault service through HTTPS. Register `https://YOUR_VAULT_HOST/auth/callback` in the Slack app's Sign in with Slack redirect configuration, then run interactively: ```sh scripts/configure-clanker-vault \ --public-url https://YOUR_VAULT_HOST \ --client-id YOUR_SLACK_APP_CLIENT_ID ``` Use the app's numeric client ID. The script prompts privately for the client secret if it is absent. It writes configuration for loopback port `8767` by default; it does not deploy the HTTPS proxy or restart the gateway. Run the proxy and gateway, then verify the public `/health` endpoint, Slack OIDC callback and an owner-bound access request. A temporary tunnel's hostname can change. Keep the registered callback and local vault origin synchronized; links already sent to Slack retain their old URLs. ## Remote Browser Tool The configured remote path uses the consumer Browser Tool connection. It requires Slack membership, the hosted vault configuration, and an isolated authorized Composio CLI setup directory containing its private `user_data.json`: ```sh scripts/configure-clanker-cloud-browser \ --provider browser_tool \ --cli-home /ABSOLUTE/PATH/TO/AUTHORIZED/COMPOSIO/SETUP ``` The script resolves the consumer project and requires instant billing to be disabled before saving configuration. It does not create the consumer account or its browser connection. Inspect `--help` for the separate managed Browser Use provider options. That paid provider is not required by the current consumer path. Composio and Browser Tool receive remote credentials and may retain arguments. Provider isolation and cookie deletion remain unresolved; use disposable accounts until the acceptance checks in the [invitation decision](decisions/2026-10-06-vault-invitations.md) pass. ## Start and check ```sh scripts/hermes-lab gateway run -v ``` Keep that foreground process open. In a second terminal: ```sh scripts/hermes-lab gateway status ``` Check member provisioning, a DM browser task and a channel mention using public pages. Inspect the actual page and reply destination. For an intentional restart, account for active work first, then use `scripts/hermes-lab gateway run -v --replace`. No system service is required for this local POC. # Clanker assignment demo Record Clanker's real flight task in Slack. yyoreel captures the interaction; Clanker performs the flight work. Checkout has not yet been reached. ## Task prompt > book me a flight to BOM. departure 7th oct. Use that exact opening message. Let Clanker ask for missing information in its next turn, and let the owner answer naturally. Do not add the origin, website, passenger count, access instructions or desired reply format to the opening prompt. ## Recording context The owner selected Nagpur (NGP) → Mumbai (BOM), 7 October 2026, on goindigo.in. These details are available for the owner's answers if Clanker asks; they are not a scripted sequence of follow-up messages. Do not assume a passenger count. The recording stops at checkout. The owner does not approve or submit a payment. This is the demo's operating limit, not an instruction added to the opening message. ## Capture sequence — approximately two minutes 1. **The request:** show the owner sending the exact short prompt to Clanker in Slack. 2. **The conversation:** show Clanker's actual follow-up questions, the owner's natural answers, and Clanker doing the task in its browser session. 3. **Private handoff:** show an actual request for access or required traveler details, owner completion, and Clanker resuming. Exclude secret entry, verification codes and personal contact details from the submitted cut. 4. **The result:** show the checkout reached by Clanker and independently inspect its route, date, flight and total. 5. **The stopping point:** show Clanker's actual checkout update or request for purchase approval. End there without approving payment or scripting its reply. These are capture beats, not prescribed dialogue. Follow the actual conversation rather than forcing each beat. Keep useful evidence of the real run. Long waits may be shortened in the edited submission. Do not replace Clanker's work with a separate scripted booking, fabricate a private handoff, or present a reenactment as a live agent result. ## Visual settings - Autozoom: on. - Keystroke HUD: on. - Background: the owner's original attached image at assets/background.png, preserved without pixel changes. It is hard-linked to the attachment to avoid duplicating image data on the full disk; deleting the temporary attachment name will not remove this asset. - Desktop CSS viewport: 1920 × 1080, 16:9, with mobile emulation disabled. - Maximum yyoreel quality: 100, giving 2× capture and 3840 × 2160 output. - Frame rate: 60 fps. - Slack: dark mode verified in the live Clanker conversation on 7 October 2026, both visually and through its sk-client-theme--dark page class. The recording config checks that class and the real Clanker composer before capture. yyoreel.config.json now contains only the read-only Slack style check. Already performed message steps are archived in recorded-config.json; do not replay them. The opening prompt was sent once with a real @Clanker mention. Authentication was verified in the Chromium recording session. The disk became full during setup; 13 GiB free was rechecked before capture. Three generated PNG source videos were later compressed with lossless RGB encoding, recovering about 3.5 GiB. RGB frame hashes at 0, 5 and 10 seconds matched before and after compression. No unrelated files were removed. The live helper stops extending a segment after two minutes or below 5 GiB free; configured actions still finish. ## Recording preparation yyoreel 0.3.3 is installed. Prepare the recorder around the actual Slack conversation, Clanker-controlled browser view and private handoff. For web surfaces, use yyoreel's Chromium pipeline with a verified recording-session login and explicit waits and assertions at handoffs. Keep secrets out of recorder configurations. The exact capture targets and timing come from the live Clanker rehearsal. No direct airline-site recorder is part of this demo. ## State The task was sent to #clanker-test on 7 October 2026. The real thread is https://clanker-global.slack.com/archives/C0C6J277ZNG/p1791380744600999. The owner confirmed NGP, 7 October 2026 and one-way. Clanker listed a 10:10 pm option for ₹6,277 and an 8:45 pm IndiGo option for ₹6,594. After the first selection, Clanker reported the 10:10 pm flight was Air India AI2584, and goindigo.in blocked access. The owner then chose IndiGo at 8:45 pm. Clanker again reported “Something went wrong” and asked to use another booking site. The owner suggested Google Flights; that preference was sent in the same thread, retaining the checkout limit. These prices and site outcomes are Clanker's reports, not independently confirmed booking facts. The displayed airline redaction is preserved as it appeared in Slack. No checkout, traveler handoff, booking or payment has been completed. Clanker subsequently reported that the 8:45 pm IndiGo flight no longer appeared in Google Flights. It offered the 10:10 pm Air India option at ₹6,277 instead; the owner has been asked whether to switch. The unavailable-flight reply is being captured as the actual outcome of this attempt. ## Capture recovery and evidence The first capture failed to save after the recorder's ten-second shutdown limit. Later screencast sources were cropped by the visible browser window; a decoded export exposed black padding and missing right-hand content. These clips are diagnostic evidence, not submission-ready footage. Do not reenact or resend the opening request to conceal this failure. A local copy of yyoreel's runtime uses full-viewport screenshot capture, a longer encoder shutdown allowance, bounded decoder threads and an optimized visible-area compositor. The installed package and Clanker product code were not changed. The compositor's pixels matched its original implementation at zoom scales 1 and 2 on a real frame and the owner's background. The corrected source is 3840 × 2160 at 60 fps. A read-only recording shows the actual conversation already present in Slack; it must be described as a thread review, not original live typing. The Google Flights follow-up was captured as a real new message. Both corrected clips passed full decode validation and visual checks. Autozoom is enabled in their timelines; the follow-up's rendered Enter HUD was inspected. The blocked outcome is not a completed checkout demo. ## Current draft assignment-demo-draft.mp4 contains the real thread review, the new Google Flights message, and Clanker's unavailable-flight reply. It is 33.07 seconds, 3840 × 2160, 60 fps and 166,446,800 bytes. The clips were joined without re-encoding. The joined draft passed a full decode check, and each segment was visually inspected. This is a draft of the blocked attempt, not evidence that checkout was reached, and it has not been uploaded or submitted.

Bind authorized profile and task"] Routing --> Queue["Durable task queue + scheduler

Hermes + Browser Use driver + local Chromium
One authorized private or shared context"] Queue -->|Pending demand| Pool["VM pool manager / autoscaler

Keys inaccessible to agent code"] Access -->|Authorized credential operation| Trusted Trusted -->|Resume after durable save| Queue Worker -->|Persist result| Delivery["Result delivery + owner-bound approval enforcement"] Delivery --> Gateway ``` These boxes describe responsibilities, not mandatory separate services. # Vault invitations and requester authorization

The vault has one **Invite to vault** button. The owner chooses a current Slack
member, checks which saved logins, API keys and payment cards to share, then
confirms use of only that selection on their behalf. Nothing is checked for a
new member, and credentials added later stay private. **People with access**
groups each member's shared credentials; **Edit access** reopens the checklist
with that member's existing selection, and **Remove** revokes their access.
The member sees **Shared with you** in their vault. An
invitation takes effect immediately; it does not send an external Slack message.
The saved credential remains in the owner's encrypted native vault. The guest
receives a grant handle and metadata, not a copied vault entry.

This implements explicit delegation. It does **not** establish that the reported
Gmail disclosure is fixed in the running system. The gateway has not been
reloaded, no real invitation has been created, and the consumer browser
provider's isolation and cookie-deletion behavior remain unverified.

## Permission boundary

Slack OIDC establishes the owner of the vault web session. Owner and workspace
come from that session, never request-body fields. CSRF and exact-origin checks
cover invite and revoke. Only native items in that owner's vault can be invited;
guests cannot pass an invited handle to create another invitation.

A durable grant binds workspace, owner, recipient and selected credential.
Saving a member's checklist validates the entire selection and applies all
permission additions/removals in one database transaction. Invalid or foreign
items cause no partial changes. Still-selected credentials retain their grant
handles; unchecked credentials and their pending approvals are revoked before
browser cleanup. Selecting credentials grants no wildcard access to the vault.
Its identity binding includes kind, origin, account identifier and creation
time. The runtime resolves that grant for the authenticated requesting member,
checks current membership of both parties, and verifies the selected native item
still exists with that binding. An unrelated native handle, another member's
grant, a removed or changed account, or a disabled member is denied. Reinvitation
after revocation produces a new grant handle.

These are credential-use permissions. A login can provide the full website
account access available to that login; an API key can provide the permissions
the service gives that key. The implementation does not impose a new read-only
role inside either service. Preventing onward grants is an application rule;
it is not a guarantee that an authorized recipient cannot copy account data or
that a third-party browser provider cannot access an entered credential.

## Execution

Logins fill the requester's supervised local browser, after exact origin and
supported-field inspection. The selected owner password is supplied by the
trusted backend, without switching the active Hermes home to the owner. Owner
TOTP or a hosted owner-only code form can satisfy verification. The one-use code
is consumed in the original requester's task, and automatic resume retains that
requester's source, home and DM.

API requests use `clanker_api_request`: the backend adds the owned or invited key
to a supported authentication header. Calls accept relative paths on the saved
HTTPS origin, reject authentication/Host/Cookie overrides, reject private or
local DNS addresses, pin the connection to a resolved public IP, and verify TLS
against the original hostname. Redirects do not forward authentication. Request
and response sizes are limited. Key values are registered for redaction and
scrubbed from responses. Synthetic transport tests verify these restrictions;
no real external API operation was performed for this change.

Cards use only the requester's supervised local checkout. An invitation lets
the member request a purchase; each exact purchase still needs the **card
owner's** hosted approval and current CVV. The owner sees merchant, order, total,
checkout text and requester. Approval does not transfer the task to the owner.
The handler rechecks the original browser, task, conversation and checkout,
consumes approval and CVV before fill/submission, and refuses replay. Submitted
is not paid; the merchant receipt must be checked. Unsupported payment frames,
wallets, subscriptions and bank approval retain their existing limits.

## Revocation and cookies

Revocation is committed before cleanup and cancels pending delegated code/card
approvals. Secret-bearing browser use is recorded before handoff, with an atomic
active-grant check. This covers a revoke racing between handle resolution and
the usage record. Work already in flight may finish before interruption; the
implementation cannot undo earlier disclosures or completed external actions.

For local Chromium, revoke interrupts the original requester task, closes their
private browsers and deletes their Chromium cookie profile under the guest
execution lock. Cleanup conservatively removes all of that recipient's private
browser state, including sessions used for other valid grants. It preserves the
owner's browser and native vault. An active grant can be used again in a fresh
guest browser after cleanup. API requests have no reusable browser cookies.

If cleanup fails, the grant remains revoked and the recorded usage keeps future
browser/terminal execution blocked. The web UI shows **cleanup pending** and
offers retry. **People with access** also exposes orphan invitations whose
native credential was removed, so that member's access can still be removed or
cleanup retried.

Consumer Browser Tool exposes task stop but no reviewed cookie/session deletion
operation. Its stop result now reports `profile_retained: null` (unknown),
correcting the previous unsupported claim of cookie deletion. A required purge
stops the task, keeps a blocked tombstone, and returns cleanup pending. Repeated
stop/retry does not clear that block. Operator cleanup needs an actual provider
deletion/reconciliation capability before a verified reset can be recorded;
this implementation does not supply that capability.

## Browser routing and unresolved incident work

New cloud state keys include workspace, authenticated requester and resolved
home, independent of the short session name or a shared conversation profile.
State carries an explicit owner marker. Provider session IDs are recorded with
that owner/context, and a recorded collision is refused and quarantined. Legacy
state is not silently adopted by the new namespace. Unknown dispatch outcomes
retain their retry block.

These controls govern Clanker's assignments and known grants. They do not prove
a fresh remote browser lacks another account's pre-existing cookies. Provider
ownership collisions are detected on acknowledgement, after task dispatch;
that check cannot undo observations the provider made before acknowledging.
Free-form remote task instructions are not an account-authorization boundary.
The reported disclosure therefore still requires tracing and invalidating
affected legacy/provider state, a provider-enforced requester isolation and
pre-read authorization design, and real two-requester/DM-handoff acceptance.
Existing login state alone must never be used as permission.

## Verified locally

The canonical Hermes test runner passed **79 tests across five affected files**:
invitations, vault, payments, consumer Browser Tool and managed cloud browser.
Coverage includes all three credential kinds, owner/recipient/workspace checks,
CSRF and forged identity fields, persistence, onward-sharing denial, revoked
access, cleanup failure, same session names/shared profile names, recorded
provider-session collisions, delegated code and payment resume, origin-bound
API requests, TLS/DNS pinning and redirect rejection. Checklist coverage adds
multi-credential sharing, atomic rejection without partial permission changes,
stable handles for retained credentials, revocation of unchecked items, no
automatic sharing of later credentials, and removal of an inactive member.

The actual sandboxed Chromium probe exercised A → B → A with two disposable
homes: owner login, denial of the owner's raw handle to the guest, invited login
fill, owner-only HTTP approval, one guest dummy checkout with an observed dummy
receipt, payment replay denial, CVV consumption, no copied guest vault entry,
guest cookie-profile removal when the login is unchecked in that member's
selection, and preservation of the owner's browser.
The same guest task/session can start a fresh browser after cleanup, while the
revoked login remains denied and an unrelated active card grant remains listed.
Its receipt is
[`2026-10-06-invitation-local-browser.json`](../../verification/evidence/2026-10-06-invitation-local-browser.json).

The visible UI check uses disposable identities and dummy credentials on
loopback. The owner initially selected login and API key; the guest saw those
two entries and no card. Edit access restored that checklist; unchecking the
login and checking the card made guest reload show only API key and card, with
the per-purchase owner-approval label. Desktop and mobile checklists and the
member-level sharing list were visually checked. Removing the member through
the single member row then made guest reload show no saved or invited access.
Screenshots are saved as
`output/playwright/vault-invite-selection-desktop.png`,
`vault-edit-selection-mobile.png` and `vault-sharing-members-mobile.png`.
Earlier per-credential Invite
screenshots represent the superseded design. The missing favicon is unrelated
to invitation behavior.
No mailbox content, real credential, live Slack message, real card
charge or production configuration change is used as verification evidence.
# Generic API-key collection template, 5 October 2026

Implemented a separate `api_key` form in the hosted vault page. The request's
`label` supplies its heading, so the template has no built-in provider name.
It accepts one masked API key, supports reveal/hide and save retry, and uses the
existing Vault updated confirmation and private Slack return link.

The existing request tool accepts `kind: api_key`, a label and an exact HTTPS API
origin without opening a browser. The trusted handler sends the private link.
The submitted key is encrypted in its owner's native vault, and durable task
resumption carries only its handle and metadata. Management lists safe metadata
and removes keys. Browser password/code filling rejects API-key handles.

## Verification

The canonical Hermes runner passed **28 tests, zero failures, zero retries**:

```sh
cd hermes
scripts/run_tests.sh ../verification/probes/test_clanker_vault.py tests/agent/test_vault_store.py --file-retries 0 -q
```

New integration coverage exercises the authenticated gateway tool context,
private-link creation, real HTTP identity/CSRF and cross-kind checks, encrypted
saves across two native owner homes (A → B → A), replacement, replay rejection,
restart/resume to the correct DM, crash-gap recovery and owner-scoped removal.
The Slack transport is a fixture; these tests send no real Slack messages.

Playwright CLI checked the real local page against the isolated dummy-data UI
fixture. Request-defined titles **Orbit API key** and **Nimbus API key** rendered
correctly. The password/code forms remained hidden. Reveal/hide worked, a
deliberate first-save failure retained the masked dummy key and allowed retry,
and success cleared the input and access token and focused the confirmation.
Management displayed API-key metadata. The 390 × 844 mobile page had no
horizontal overflow. No real credential or external API call was used.

- [Desktop template](../../output/playwright/clanker-api-key-template-desktop.png)
- [Mobile template](../../output/playwright/clanker-api-key-template-mobile.png)
- [Saved confirmation](../../output/playwright/clanker-api-key-saved-desktop.png)

Native changes are reproducible through `patches/hermes/api-key-vault.patch`
after the hosted-vault patch. Reverse applicability checks passed for both.

## Remaining work

This implements API-key collection and storage. Authenticated API execution from
saved handles is still unimplemented. The live gateway was not restarted or
tested with a real Slack request. It needs a restart and a new task to load the
updated request schema and prompt; this receipt establishes local acceptance.

come from that session, never request-body fields. CSRF and exact-origin checks
cover invite and revoke. Only native items in that owner's vault can be invited;
guests cannot pass an invited handle to create another invitation.

A durable grant binds workspace, owner, recipient and selected credential.
Saving a member's checklist validates the entire selection and applies all
permission additions/removals in one database transaction. Invalid or foreign
items cause no partial changes. Still-selected credentials retain their grant
handles; unchecked credentials and their pending approvals are revoked before
browser cleanup. Selecting credentials grants no wildcard access to the vault.
Its identity binding includes kind, origin, account identifier and creation
time. The runtime resolves that grant for the authenticated requesting member,
checks current membership of both parties, and verifies the selected native item
still exists with that binding. An unrelated native handle, another member's
grant, a removed or changed account, or a disabled member is denied. Reinvitation
after revocation produces a new grant handle.

These are credential-use permissions. A login can provide the full website
account access available to that login; an API key can provide the permissions
the service gives that key. The implementation does not impose a new read-only
role inside either service. Preventing onward grants is an application rule;
it is not a guarantee that an authorized recipient cannot copy account data or
that a third-party browser provider cannot access an entered credential.

## Execution

Logins fill the requester's supervised local browser, after exact origin and
supported-field inspection. The selected owner password is supplied by the
trusted backend, without switching the active Hermes home to the owner. Owner
TOTP or a hosted owner-only code form can satisfy verification. The one-use code
is consumed in the original requester's task, and automatic resume retains that
requester's source, home and DM.

API requests use `clanker_api_request`: the backend adds the owned or invited key
to a supported authentication header. Calls accept relative paths on the saved
HTTPS origin, reject authentication/Host/Cookie overrides, reject private or
local DNS addresses, pin the connection to a resolved public IP, and verify TLS
against the original hostname. Redirects do not forward authentication. Request
and response sizes are limited. Key values are registered for redaction and
scrubbed from responses. Synthetic transport tests verify these restrictions;
no real external API operation was performed for this change.

Cards use only the requester's supervised local checkout. An invitation lets
the member request a purchase; each exact purchase still needs the **card
owner's** hosted approval and current CVV. The owner sees merchant, order, total,
checkout text and requester. Approval does not transfer the task to the owner.
The handler rechecks the original browser, task, conversation and checkout,
consumes approval and CVV before fill/submission, and refuses replay. Submitted
is not paid; the merchant receipt must be checked. Unsupported payment frames,
wallets, subscriptions and bank approval retain their existing limits.

## Revocation and cookies

Revocation is committed before cleanup and cancels pending delegated code/card
approvals. Secret-bearing browser use is recorded before handoff, with an atomic
active-grant check. This covers a revoke racing between handle resolution and
the usage record. Work already in flight may finish before interruption; the
implementation cannot undo earlier disclosures or completed external actions.

For local Chromium, revoke interrupts the original requester task, closes their
private browsers and deletes their Chromium cookie profile under the guest
execution lock. Cleanup conservatively removes all of that recipient's private
browser state, including sessions used for other valid grants. It preserves the
owner's browser and native vault. An active grant can be used again in a fresh
guest browser after cleanup. API requests have no reusable browser cookies.

If cleanup fails, the grant remains revoked and the recorded usage keeps future
browser/terminal execution blocked. The web UI shows **cleanup pending** and
offers retry. **People with access** also exposes orphan invitations whose
native credential was removed, so that member's access can still be removed or
cleanup retried.

Consumer Browser Tool exposes task stop but no reviewed cookie/session deletion
operation. Its stop result now reports `profile_retained: null` (unknown),
correcting the previous unsupported claim of cookie deletion. A required purge
stops the task, keeps a blocked tombstone, and returns cleanup pending. Repeated
stop/retry does not clear that block. Operator cleanup needs an actual provider
deletion/reconciliation capability before a verified reset can be recorded;
this implementation does not supply that capability.

## Browser routing and unresolved incident work

New cloud state keys include workspace, authenticated requester and resolved
home, independent of the short session name or a shared conversation profile.
State carries an explicit owner marker. Provider session IDs are recorded with
that owner/context, and a recorded collision is refused and quarantined. Legacy
state is not silently adopted by the new namespace. Unknown dispatch outcomes
retain their retry block.

These controls govern Clanker's assignments and known grants. They do not prove
a fresh remote browser lacks another account's pre-existing cookies. Provider
ownership collisions are detected on acknowledgement, after task dispatch;
that check cannot undo observations the provider made before acknowledging.
Free-form remote task instructions are not an account-authorization boundary.
The reported disclosure therefore still requires tracing and invalidating
affected legacy/provider state, a provider-enforced requester isolation and
pre-read authorization design, and real two-requester/DM-handoff acceptance.
Existing login state alone must never be used as permission.

## Verified locally

The canonical Hermes test runner passed **79 tests across five affected files**:
invitations, vault, payments, consumer Browser Tool and managed cloud browser.
Coverage includes all three credential kinds, owner/recipient/workspace checks,
CSRF and forged identity fields, persistence, onward-sharing denial, revoked
access, cleanup failure, same session names/shared profile names, recorded
provider-session collisions, delegated code and payment resume, origin-bound
API requests, TLS/DNS pinning and redirect rejection. Checklist coverage adds
multi-credential sharing, atomic rejection without partial permission changes,
stable handles for retained credentials, revocation of unchecked items, no
automatic sharing of later credentials, and removal of an inactive member.

The actual sandboxed Chromium probe exercised A → B → A with two disposable
homes: owner login, denial of the owner's raw handle to the guest, invited login
fill, owner-only HTTP approval, one guest dummy checkout with an observed dummy
receipt, payment replay denial, CVV consumption, no copied guest vault entry,
guest cookie-profile removal when the login is unchecked in that member's
selection, and preservation of the owner's browser.
